Maul
MAWL
noun
From the Latin malleus, a hammer, through the Old French mail — the same root as mallet and malleable. A maul is a heavy hammer or war-club, a weapon of crushing rather than cutting.

Biblical Definition

Solomon names three weapons in a single verse and assigns all of them to one sin: “A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow” (Pro 25:18). The three are chosen with care, for they cover every range and every kind of wound. The maul crushes at close quarters, the sword cuts at arm’s length, and the sharp arrow strikes a man who never saw the archer. So the false witness destroys near and far, openly and invisibly, and the proverb does not say he is like these things — it says he is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow. The man is the weapon. This sits within the ninth commandment’s wide reach, which Scripture applies not only to formal perjury but to the whole traffic of the tongue: talebearing, whispering, backbiting, and the report passed on without inquiry. Solomon elsewhere sets the alternative plainly: “There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health” (Pro 12:18). Two tongues, two effects, and no neutral ground. What is said of a neighbour either wounds him or heals him, and the speaker is choosing his instrument every time he opens his mouth.

Webster 1828 Definition

A heavy hammer or war-club used for crushing; in Proverbs, one of three weapons the false witness is said to be.

MAUL, n. A heavy wooden hammer; a beetle; anciently, a club or mace used in war.

From the Latin malleus, a hammer; Old French mail.

Of the same family as mallet, malleable, and malleus.

MAUL, v.t. To beat and bruise with a heavy instrument; to wound grossly.

Pro 25:18 sets it with the sword and the arrow as the arms of a false witness.

Key Scripture

Pro 25:18 — "A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour is a maul, and a sword, and a sharp arrow."

Exo 20:16 — "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour."

Pro 12:18 — "There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health."

Pro 18:8 — "The words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly."

Modern Corruption

The ninth commandment is widely narrowed to courtroom perjury, leaving gossip, the unverified report, and the passed-on rumour untouched — though these are precisely the maul’s ordinary work.

expand to see more

The corruption is the shrinking of the ninth commandment to a legal technicality. Most people, asked whether they have borne false witness, think of a witness box and answer no with a clear conscience. Solomon has a wider field in view, and so does the whole of Scripture: thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; the words of a talebearer are as wounds, and they go down into the innermost parts of the belly (Pro 18:8); backbiters are listed among those given over in Rom 1. The commandment governs everything said against a neighbour, and the modern machinery for saying it — the forwarded message, the anonymous account, the story repeated because it is interesting — has enlarged the maul’s reach beyond anything Solomon saw.

Recover the plain sense: the test is not merely is it true but is it mine to say, to this person, for this reason. A true report circulated to wound is still a weapon, and Pro 18:8 warns that such words are received eagerly and lodge deep, which is why retraction never undoes them. Set against it the alternative Solomon names: the tongue of the wise is health. That is the striking thing about Pro 12:18 — speech is never inert. It is either piercing or healing, maul or medicine, and the same mouth is capable of both. The ninth commandment does not merely forbid the weapon; it puts a physician’s instrument in your hand instead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin malleus, a hammer — a crushing club; one of the three weapons Solomon says a false witness is.

expand to see more

Maul — Latin malleus, a hammer; Old French mail.

Kin to mallet and malleable.

A crushing weapon, used at close quarters, unlike the sword or arrow.

Pro 25:18 covers every range: maul near, sword at arm’s length, arrow unseen.

The proverb does not say like a maul — the man is the weapon.

Usage

"Three weapons, one sin: false witness wounds near, far, and invisibly."

"The ninth commandment reaches talebearing and backbiting, not only perjury."

"Pro 12:18 gives the alternative — the tongue of the wise is health."
